es.summary: Acumulación de amoníaco en sangre por insuficiencia hepática o renal que atraviesa la barrera hematoencefálica y produce encefalopatía.
key_points: El hígado convierte amoníaco en urea; su falla genera hiperamonemia.
Manifestaciones neurológicas incluyen confusión, asterixis y coma.
Lactulosa y rifaximina reducen la producción de amoníaco.
Diálisis se reserva para niveles muy altos o deterioro neurológico.
Control estricto de electrolitos y balance hídrico es esencial.

pathophysiology: El hígado transforma NH3 en urea mediante el ciclo de la urea.
Insuficiencia hepática o shunts portosistémicos impiden esta conversión.
El amoníaco se acumula en sangre y cruza la barrera hematoencefálica.
En el SNC altera neurotransmisores y provoca edema cerebral.
risk_factors: Sangrado gastrointestinal con alto aporte proteico.
Dieta alta en proteínas o ayuno prolongado.
Uso de diuréticos que aumentan catabolismo proteico.
signs_symptoms: Alteración del estado mental: confusión, somnolencia.
diagnostics: Pruebas de función hepática elevadas (AST, ALT, bilirrubina).
Imagen cerebral (TC/MRI) si se sospecha edema.
treatment: Lactulosa oral/rectal para reducir producción de amoníaco.
Rifaximina para disminuir bacterias productoras de amoníaco.
Restricción de proteínas a 0.6‑0.8 g/kg/día según estado.
Diálisis (hemodiálisis o hemodiafiltración) si niveles >150 mg/dL o coma.
Corrección de electrolitos y soporte hemodinámico.
complications: Edema cerebral y riesgo de herniación.
nursing_care: Monitorear nivel de conciencia (Escala de Glasgow) cada hora.
Vigilar signos vitales, especialmente presión arterial y frecuencia respiratoria.
Administrar lactulosa según orden y observar diarrea.
Controlar ingesta de proteínas y registrar alimentos.
Preparar al paciente para posible diálisis.
patient_teaching: Explicar la dieta baja en proteínas y su importancia.
Instruir sobre el uso correcto de lactulosa y signos de diarrea excesiva.
Señalar síntomas de empeoramiento (confusión, somnolencia) y cuándo buscar ayuda.
Promover adherencia a citas médicas y pruebas de laboratorio.

en.summary: Accumulation of ammonia in the blood due to liver or kidney failure that crosses the blood‑brain barrier and causes encephalopathy.
key_points: The liver converts ammonia to urea; failure generates hyperammonemia.
Neurologic manifestations include confusion, asterixis, and coma.
Lactulose and rifaximin reduce ammonia production.
Dialysis is reserved for very high levels or neurologic deterioration.
Strict control of electrolytes and fluid balance is essential.

pathophysiology: The liver transforms NH3 into urea via the urea cycle.
Hepatic failure or portosystemic shunts prevent this conversion.
Ammonia accumulates in the blood and crosses the blood‑brain barrier.
In the CNS it alters neurotransmitters and causes cerebral edema.
risk_factors: Gastrointestinal bleeding with high protein intake.
Use of diuretics that increase protein catabolism.
diagnostics: Elevated liver function tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin).
Brain imaging (CT/MRI) if cerebral edema is suspected.
treatment: Oral/rectal lactulose to reduce ammonia production.
Protein restriction to 0.6‑0.8 g/kg/day based on status.
Dialysis (hemodialysis or hemodiafiltration) if levels >150 mg/dL or coma.
Correct electrolytes and provide hemodynamic support.
complications: Cerebral edema and risk of herniation.
nursing_care: Monitor level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale) hourly.
Monitor vital signs, especially blood pressure and respiratory rate.
Administer lactulose per order and observe for diarrhea.
Control protein intake and record foods.
patient_teaching: Explain low‑protein diet and its importance.
Instruct on proper lactulose use and signs of excessive diarrhea.
Highlight worsening symptoms (confusion, drowsiness) and when to seek help.
Encourage adherence to medical appointments and lab tests.

key_points.5.quote: Management of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting includes efforts to maintain client comfort, adequate hydration, and electrolyte balance.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: It should be noted that any client with liver disease or cirrhosis can have decreased metabolic activity, making them more susceptible to dose-related side effects if they are taking a medication metabolized through the liver.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Chemotherapy-associated nausea and vomiting is another common side effect and can vary from drug to drug and client to client.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: Fludarabine causes severe central nervous system toxicity, including blindness, coma, seizures, and death.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: Aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT) are two common liver enzymes to monitor because the elevation of these enzymes may indicate hepatic dysfunction or liver damage.

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: Understand the need for frequent follow-up and laboratory tests.
